name: Hyde Park
headline: Three commuter rail lines, Mother Brook
and the Neponset River at the city's southern edge.
answer: Hyde Park is Boston's southernmost neighborhood, 7.9 miles south of downtown, incorporated as a town in 1868 from parts of Dorchester, Dedham and Milton and annexed to Boston in 1912. Single-family and two-family homes made up nearly three-quarters of its housing units in the city's open space plan, and the Boston Planning & Development Agency counted 33,009 people there in 2020. Three commuter rail lines stop at its Hyde Park, Fairmount and Readville stations.
meta: Hyde Park, Boston: a former town with Cleary Square, Victorian Fairmount Hill and Readville, three commuter rail lines and the Stony Brook Reservation.

boundaries.text: Hyde Park is Boston's southernmost neighborhood. The George Wright Golf Course lies partly in Hyde Park and partly in Roslindale, the Stony Brook Reservation runs south from West Roxbury to Mother Brook in Hyde Park, and the city's open space plan places Hyde Park's eastern sections next to Mattapan. In Readville it meets Milton to the south and Dedham to the west. Hyde Park Avenue and the Amtrak and MBTA tracks cross the neighborhood, with most of its open space to their west.

overview: Hyde Park was assembled from the edges of three older towns: Grew's Woods in Dorchester, Fairmount in Milton and Readville in Dedham. Mother Brook, ordered dug in 1639 to divert Charles River water to the Neponset, powered mills in what is now Readville, which was called Dedham Low Plains until 1847, when it was renamed for James Read of the Dedham Manufacturing Company. Henry Grew settled there in 1847, rail lines extended from Boston in the 1850s, and in 1856 Alpheus P. Blake's Fairmount Land Company and Twenty Associates bought 100 acres and began building houses. On April 22, 1868, the Town of Hyde Park was incorporated in Norfolk County from about 1,300 acres of Dorchester, 800 of Dedham and 700 of Milton. Its voters chose to join Boston in 1912.

Cleary Square and Logan Square frame the central business district, and the Hyde Park Branch Library, which opened in its present building in September 1899 and became a Boston Public Library branch at annexation, is the only branch that began as a town library. Fairmount Hill, on a hillside above the Neponset River, keeps late-19th- and early-20th-century houses in Italianate, Gothic Revival and Victorian styles. Readville was industrial: Camp Meigs trained Union regiments there from 1862 to 1865, including the 54th Massachusetts; the Readville Trotting Park followed on the site until 1937; the B.F. Sturtevant Company had a 20-acre plant employing 1,500 people by 1912; and the New Haven Railroad's locomotive and car shops ran until 1960.

Boston's 2008-2014 open space plan counted single-family homes as 48% of Hyde Park's housing units and two-family homes as 24%, and found most of its open space west of Hyde Park Avenue and the rail line; the state Department of Conservation and Recreation held 470 acres in the neighborhood, mainly in the Stony Brook and Neponset River reservations. A rezoning begun in April 2008 was approved by the Boston Zoning Commission in February 2012. Cleary Square is now the subject of a Squares + Streets small area plan: the Planning Department released a draft plan and zoning map on March 17, 2026, followed by a revised draft.

housing.text: Hyde Park's housing is mainly single-family and two-family homes: Boston's 2008-2014 open space plan put single-family homes at 48% of units and two-family homes at 24%, nearly three-quarters together. Fairmount Hill keeps houses in late-19th- and early-20th-century styles, including Italianate, Gothic Revival and Victorian. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 59.5% of occupied units as owner-occupied (7,893 units), compared with 35.3% citywide.

areas.name: Cleary Square and Logan Square
areas.line: The two squares between which Hyde Park's central business district lies; Cleary Square is the focus of a draft Squares + Streets plan released in 2026.

areas.name: Fairmount Hill
areas.line: A hillside above the Neponset River, laid out from 1856 by the Fairmount Land Company, with late-19th- and early-20th-century Italianate, Gothic Revival and Victorian houses; Fairmount station sits at Fairmount Avenue and the Truman Highway.

areas.name: Readville
areas.line: The southern section, formerly Dedham Low Plains, bordered by Milton and Dedham, with Wolcott Square, Readville station at 1800 Hyde Park Avenue, a commuter rail maintenance and layover yard, and the Neponset River and Fowl Meadow wetlands.

commute.text: The Fairmount Line runs from Readville through Fairmount and six more stops to South Station, and Fairmount station is in fare zone 1A. Hyde Park station, at 1 Pingree Street and reached by ramps from the River Street bridge, is a Providence/Stoughton Line stop with some Franklin/Foxboro trains, running to Ruggles, Back Bay and South Station; Readville, at 1800 Hyde Park Avenue, is the outer terminus for most Fairmount trains and a Franklin/Foxboro stop. MBTA bus routes connect the neighborhood with the subway at Forest Hills and Mattapan.

places.name: Stony Brook Reservation
places.line: A 616-acre DCR reservation, one of the five original reservations of the Metropolitan Park Commission, running south from Washington Street in West Roxbury to Mother Brook in Hyde Park, with hiking and biking trails, fishing at Turtle Pond and an ice rink.

places.name: George Wright Golf Course
places.line: An 18-hole City of Boston course designed by Donald Ross and opened on April 23, 1938, at 420 West Street, on 156 acres enclosed by a stone wall.

places.name: Mother Brook
places.line: A canal ordered by Dedham in 1639 and flowing by 1641, about 3.6 miles long, carrying Charles River water to the Neponset River in Hyde Park; the page calls it the first man-made canal in the present-day United States, and it now forms part of a flood-control system.

places.name: Camp Meigs Park
places.line: A park of nearly three acres at 11 Stanbro Street in Readville, on part of the Civil War training camp, dedicated by the Commonwealth on July 11, 1903, with a cannon-shaped granite monument and a later marker to the regiments that trained there, among them the 54th and 55th Massachusetts Infantry and 5th Massachusetts Cavalry.

places.name: Hyde Park Branch Library
places.line: Opened in its present building in September 1899 as the town library, which had started in 1873; it joined the Boston Public Library at annexation in 1912, and a January 2000 addition by Schwartz/Silver Architects doubled its size.

places.name: Neponset River Reservation
places.line: DCR land along the Neponset River, which runs past Readville and below Fairmount Hill; with Stony Brook, it accounts for most of the 470 acres the state holds in the neighborhood.

history.text: Dedham ordered Mother Brook dug to carry Charles River water to the Neponset; water was flowing by July 1641.
The Fairmount Land Company and Twenty Associates bought 100 acres and started their first house on May 15.
The Town of Hyde Park was incorporated on April 22 from parts of Dorchester, Dedham and Milton.
Hyde Park voters chose to join the City of Boston, and the town library became a Boston Public Library branch.

search_notes: A search for 'moving to Hyde Park Boston neighborhood guide' (2026-10-23) returned a 2023 WBUR locals' field guide, an apartment-rental guide and several Walk Score pages (some for Hyde Park Avenue addresses in Jamaica Plain). No guide combining the town's history, the three rail lines and Warren Group figures appeared; a sourced guide can fill that gap. 'Hyde Park MA real estate agent' was not searched.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Hyde Park?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, which lists Hyde Park on its own row, the median single-family sale price for calendar year 2025 was $675,000, across 101 sales, up from $655,000 across 118 sales in 2024. The condominium median was $482,000 across 54 sales in 2025, against $441,500 across 48 sales in 2024.

faq.q: Does Hyde Park have commuter rail?
faq.a: Yes, on three lines. The Fairmount Line stops at Fairmount and Readville, Hyde Park station is on the Providence/Stoughton Line with some Franklin/Foxboro trains, and Readville is also a Franklin/Foxboro stop. Fairmount station is in fare zone 1A.

faq.q: Which school district serves Hyde Park?
faq.a: Boston Public Schools. School assignment is set by the district; review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: When did Hyde Park become part of Boston?
faq.a: Hyde Park was incorporated as a town in Norfolk County on April 22, 1868, from parts of Dorchester, Dedham and Milton, and its voters chose to join Boston in 1912.

faq.q: Is Hyde Park getting Squares + Streets zoning?
faq.a: Cleary Square is the subject of a Squares + Streets small area plan. The Planning Department released a draft plan and zoning map on March 17, 2026, and a revised draft later in 2026; check the city's planning page for its current status.

notes: Written 2026-10-23. Population: Boston Planning & Development Agency Research Division, 'Boston in Context: Neighborhoods, 2020 Decennial Census Redistricting Data and 2016-2020 American Community Survey' (April 2022), 'Population by Age Group' table, total 33,009 (same report and neighborhood approximation as the West Roxbury and Jamaica Plain records); tenure 59.5% owner-occupied, 7,893 owner-occupied units, Boston 35.3% (Housing Tenure table). Housing shares (48% single-family, 24% two-family, 'nearly three-quarters'), the 470 DCR acres, the Hyde Park Avenue and rail line split and the eastern border with Mattapan are from Boston's Open Space Plan 2008-2014, section 7.2.8 Hyde Park (Boston Parks & Recreation; assumed to be the same 2008-2014 plan as the West Roxbury section from the file series), which rests on older census data. That plan gives the total open space inventory as both 619 and 618 acres (588 protected), so no total is used. Wikipedia's 'about 12,000 housing units, 60% owner-occupied' was not used in favor of the BPDA figures. Southernmost neighborhood, 7.9 miles from downtown, the three source towns (Grew's Woods, Fairmount, Readville), 1832-34 railroad, Henry Grew 1847, the 1912 annexation, Cleary and Logan Squares, Fairmount Hill house styles, Camp Meigs and the 54th, the Readville Trotting Park to 1937, Sturtevant's 20-acre, 1,500-employee plant 'by annexation', and the April 2008 rezoning and February 2012 Zoning Commission approval are from Wikipedia's Hyde Park article; the Boston record also gives Hyde Park (1912) as the last annexation in its list. Wikipedia's infobox gives January 1, 1912; the copy says only 1912. Incorporation date and acreages from Dorchester, Dedham and Milton, Blake, the Fairmount Land Company and the May 15, 1856 first house are from the Hyde Park Historical Society (https://www.hydeparkhistoricalsociety.org/founding/); Wikipedia's Readville article says Readville joined Hyde Park in 1867, which conflicts with the 1868 incorporation and was not used. Dedham Low Plains (1655 to 1847), James Read, the 1960 closing of the New Haven shops, the Neponset River and Fowl Meadow are from Wikipedia's Readville article. Camp Meigs 1862 to 1865 and the units from Wikipedia's Camp Meigs article; Camp Meigs Park (11 Stanbro Street, nearly three acres, dedicated July 11, 1903, cannon monument, marker) from Massachusetts Civil War Monuments Project, a secondary source; the city's parks page for it was not found. Fairmount Hill 'on a hillside overlooking the Neponset River' from WalkBoston's Hyde Park and Victorian Fairmount walking map (https://dev.walkboston.org/?p=5030); no Boston Landmark or historic district designation for Fairmount Hill was confirmed. Library from the BPL's About the Hyde Park Branch page (1873, 1884, September 1899, 1912, 'the only branch to have begun service as a town library', January 2000 addition by Schwartz/Silver); its street address and original architect were not given there and are left out. Rail: Fairmount Line stations from the MBTA timetable; Providence/Stoughton and Franklin/Foxboro stop patterns from the MBTA timetables (https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-Providence/timetable and https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-Franklin/timetable: Readville only on select Providence/Stoughton trips; Hyde Park on only a few Franklin/Foxboro trips); station addresses and zones from MBTA stop pages (Hyde Park, 1 Pingree St, zone 1, https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-NEC-2203; Readville, 1800 Hyde Park Ave, zone 2, https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-DB-0095; Fairmount, Fairmount Ave and Truman Hwy, zone 1A, https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-DB-2205); parking prices left out because they change. The River Street ramps are from Wikipedia's Hyde Park station article; the Readville layover yard from Wikipedia's Readville station article. Bus routes: Wikipedia lists 24, 32, 33, 40 and 50, connecting to Forest Hills and Mattapan; numbers left out of copy because the MBTA bus network is being redesigned. 'Truman Highway' is the MBTA's spelling for Fairmount station's cross street; no state route numbers were confirmed. Squares + Streets: the Cleary Square planning page (http://www.bostonplans.org/planning-zoning/planning-initiatives/cleary-square) lists a draft plan and zoning map dated 3/17/2026, a closeout meeting on June 17, 2026, and a revised draft labeled 10/8/2026; adoption by the board or the Zoning Commission was not shown, so the copy says only that a draft and a revised draft were released. Recheck before launch. Mother Brook (1639 order, flowing by July 14, 1641, about 3.6 miles, first man-made canal in the present-day U.S., flood control) from Wikipedia. Stony Brook Reservation from Wikipedia (616 acres, Turtle Pond, ice rink), as in the West Roxbury record. George Wright Golf Course from Wikipedia. Neponset River Reservation: no acreage for the reservation within Hyde Park was given; its course past Readville and below Fairmount Hill rests on Wikipedia's Readville article and the WalkBoston map. Schools: assignment is by address and set by Boston Public Schools; no school is named. Nearby: Roslindale, Mattapan and West Roxbury border Hyde Park; Dorchester does not, but the Fairmount Line runs through it. Market: values from tools/data/boston-neighborhood-rows-2025.json (Warren Group rows read 2026-10-23 with pdf.js; the single-family row breaks across a page, as the reading shows); 118 to 101 sales is -14.4% and $655,000 to $675,000 is 3.1%, matching the row. Region: set to 'Greater Boston' as instructed for this round; the earlier Boston neighborhood records use 'Greater Boston (the city)'. Fair housing: left out Wikipedia's material on the 1970s busing activism, the Haitian Literacy Program, the Fairmount public housing complex 'for low-income and elderly residents', foreclosure rates by section and 'limited public transit compared with other neighborhoods'; the 54th Massachusetts is named as a historic regiment, which describes the camp's history, not who lives in Hyde Park. The WalkBoston phrase 'Boston's southernmost tip' for Fairmount and Cleary Square was not used, since Readville lies farther south. Fact-check 2026-10-23: independent check against the cited sources. Verified: population 33,009 and tenure 59.5% (7,893 units; Boston 35.3%) in the BPDA April 2022 report; the open space plan's 48% single-family and 24% two-family ('nearly three-quarters'), 470 DCR acres mainly in the Stony Brook and Neponset River reservations, and open space west of Hyde Park Avenue and the Amtrak/MBTA tracks; incorporation April 22, 1868 with about 1,300 acres from Dorchester, 800 from Dedham and 700 from Milton, the 100-acre 1856 purchase and May 15, 1856 first house (Hyde Park Historical Society); Norfolk County, the vote to join Boston, the 1912 annexation (BPL page and Wikipedia), Grew 1847, Blake, Cleary and Logan Squares, Camp Meigs and the 54th, the Readville Trotting Park on the former Camp Meigs site to 1937, Sturtevant, the 2008/2012 rezoning (Wikipedia); Dedham Low Plains, James Read, the 1960 shops closing, Milton and Dedham borders (Readville Wikipedia); Fairmount Line stations Fairmount and Readville (MBTA timetable), Hyde Park a regular Providence/Stoughton stop (about 21 of 37 inbound trips) and on 3 Franklin/Foxboro trips, Readville on 6 of 37 Providence/Stoughton trips and 28 of 32 Franklin/Foxboro trips (MBTA timetables, read 2026-10-23); stop pages (Hyde Park 1 Pingree St zone 1; Readville 1800 Hyde Park Ave zone 2; Fairmount, Fairmount Ave and Truman Hwy, zone 1A); River Street ramps (Wikipedia Hyde Park station (MBTA)); Readville layover yard and outer terminus (Wikipedia Readville station); bus links to Forest Hills and Mattapan; Stony Brook Reservation, George Wright Golf Course, Mother Brook, Camp Meigs Park (address, acreage, July 11, 1903, cannon monument) and the library. The Cleary Square planning page shows only a draft (3/17/2026) and a revised draft (10/8/2026) with a June 17, 2026 closeout meeting; no adoption is shown, and the copy does not call it adopted. Corrected: the boundary paragraph, which Wikipedia did not support, is rewritten from the open space plan, the Stony Brook, George Wright and Readville articles, and its source is now the open space plan (its 'largely minority' wording about Mattapan is not used); Fairmount Hill house styles are 'late 19th and early 20th century' per Wikipedia; Mother Brook's mouth is in Hyde Park, not specifically Readville; Mother Brook was 'ordered dug' in 1639; the 1856 purchase is '100 acres' (not 'about'); the Camp Meigs Park marker is dedicated to the regiments that trained at the camp without naming them, so the units are now named as those that trained there; Readville is the outer terminus for most, not all, Fairmount trains; the Fairmount Line text no longer names Mattapan and Dorchester as places it runs through (not on the timetable). Removed: the 1832 to 1834 Boston and Providence Railroad date (in neither the Hyde Park nor the Readville article), replaced by Wikipedia's 'rail lines extended from Boston in the 1850s'; the claim that Cleary and Logan Squares sit near the library and the River Street bridge (unsourced); 'side by side through the middle' for Hyde Park Avenue and the rail line. Region set to 'Greater Boston (the city)' to match west-roxbury.json. Market matches tools/data/boston-neighborhood-rows-2025.json exactly. Still unconfirmed: the Camp Meigs site's later name (Wikipedia's Camp Meigs article says Readville Race Track; the Hyde Park article says Readville Trotting Park); the Readville 1867 vs Hyde Park 1868 conflict; Cleary Square adoption status (recheck before launch).
